newsitem.title: USA: Senate committee starts work on U.S. tax bill.
newsitem.headline: Senate committee starts work on U.S. tax bill.

text.p: The Senate Finance Committee began work Thursday on a bill that would cut taxes by a net $85 billion over five years, with both Democrats and Republicans calling it a bipartisan effort.

The tone differed from last week's session in the House Ways and Means Committee, where Democrats offered their own tax plan and voted against the Republican bill. The House committee approved that legislation, and differences with the Senate version must eventually be worked out.
"As with any bipartisan effort, not everyone will be fully satisfied with this proposal," Senate Finance Committee Chairman William Roth, a Delaware Republican, said.
"For my part, I would like to see greater tax relief, and I consider this the first in a series of steps that I hope will lead to deeper tax cuts and eventual long-term reform," he said.
Some Democrats said they preferred not to cut taxes at this time, but were obligated by last month's budget agreement between congressional leaders and the White House.

Sen. Daniel Patrick Moynihan of New York, the senior Democrat on the panel, said there was an "extraordinary spirit of cooperation" in drafting the bill. But he added that some Democrats voted against the budget agreement because "our feeling was that this was no time for a tax cut."
Senators from both parties offered 110 amendments to the bill, including five that would raise the federal tax on cigarettes.

The bill included $53 billion over five years in tax increases and revenue raisers, mainly from aviation taxes. The airline ticket tax would be extended, but the rate reduced to 7.5 percent from 10 percent for flights in rural areas.
The bill would repeal the $6 departure tax and impose a 10 percent tax on the portion of the international ticket price attributable to flights in U.S. airspace.
Senators from states with major airports said the aviation tax proposals would hurt the airline and tourism industries.

Sen. Phil Gramm, a Texas Republican, likened the international ticket tax proposal to "putting a cover charge at a department store," saying it might discourage tourism to the United States in favor of another country.
"The Canadians ought to be outside handing out tourist literature," Gramm said.
Sen. Carol Moseley-Braun, an Illinois Democrat, said the airline proposals were "penny wise and pound foolish" because they would hurt the airline and tourism industries.

The biggest piece of the proposed tax legislation would be $81 billion for a $500-per-child tax credit for children under age 17. If the child is aged 13 to 16, the tax credit must be deposited in an IRA-type account earmarked for education.
Roth's bill provided a tax credit of 50 percent of up to $3,000 college tuition and 75 percent of up to $2,000 for students attending community colleges and technical schools.

The legislation would cut the capital gains tax rate to 20 percent from a maximum 28 percent for individuals, but offered no reduction for corporations. Married couples could exclude from taxation up to $500,000 of gain from selling a home.

The threshold at which the estate tax is imposed would be gradually raised to $1 million from the current $600,000. The bill would immediately exclude up to $1 million from the inheritance tax for a family farm or business that made up more than 50 percent of the estate.

The bill proposed penalty-free withdrawals from Individual Retirement Accounts for first-time homebuying up to $10,000, people unemployed for a long time, and education expenses. Homemakers could put up to $2,000 a year in an IRA regardless of spouse participation in an employer pension plan.
The bill included funding for Amtrak, the rail service, at a cost of $2.3 billion over five years, paid by a half-cent of the 4.3 cents per gallon gasoline tax.
